abstract: Language models have graduated from being research prototypes to commercialized products offered as web APIs, and recent works have highlighted the multilingual capabilities of these products. The API vendors charge their users based on usage, more specifically on the number of “tokens” processed or generated by the underlying language models. What constitutes a token, however, is training data and model dependent with a large variance in the number of tokens required to convey the same information in different languages. In this work, we analyze the effect of this non-uniformity on the fairness of an API’s pricing policy across languages. We conduct a systematic analysis of the cost and utility of OpenAI’s language model API on multilingual benchmarks in 22 typologically diverse languages. We show evidence that speakers of a large number of the supported languages are overcharged while obtaining poorer results. These speakers tend to also come from regions where the APIs are less affordable to begin with. Through these analyses, we aim to increase transparency around language model APIs’ pricing policies and encourage the vendors to make them more equitable.

bibliographic.title: Do All Languages Cost the Same? Tokenization in the Era of Commercial Language Models

content.problem: Commercial language model APIs charge users per token, and because subword tokenizers fragment different languages and scripts at very different rates, speakers of some languages pay much more to convey the same information.
content.proposed_solution: The authors run a systematic analysis across 22 typologically diverse languages measuring tokenizer fragmentation, estimated API cost, in-context learning performance, and socio-economic affordability, to expose the unfairness of per-token API pricing.
content.algorithm_or_model: byte-level byte pair encoding (BBPE) tokenization, analyzed on ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) and BLOOMZ
dataset_testbed: CC100 (used to estimate ChatGPT pretraining language distribution)

metrics.name: relative token count
metrics.condition: Average tokens per sentence on a FLORES-200 subset tokenized with ChatGPT's tokenizer; languages with their own scripts (e.g., Telugu, Georgian) require up to 5x more tokens than Latin-script languages

metrics.name: relative API cost
metrics.condition: Estimated API usage cost for most mid-resourced Indic languages with non-Latin scripts relative to English

metrics.name: relative experiment cost
metrics.condition: Average cost of prompt plus generated tokens for XLSUM evaluations in Telugu and Amharic relative to English with ChatGPT

metrics.name: Spearman correlation (cost vs HDI)
metrics.condition: Correlation between API cost and Human Development Index across languages for XLSUM

metrics.name: Spearman correlation (cost vs HDI)
metrics.condition: Correlation between API cost and Human Development Index across languages for XFACT

metrics.name: Spearman correlation (cost vs utility)
metrics.condition: Correlation between API cost and model utility across languages for XFACT

metrics.name: Pearson correlation (cost vs HDI)
metrics.condition: Correlation between API cost and Human Development Index across languages for XFACT

content.claim: Speakers of many supported non-Latin-script languages are overcharged by commercial LM APIs while receiving poorer in-context learning performance, and this double unfairness falls hardest on populations in less economically developed countries.
author_stated_limitations: The FLORES-200 parallel corpus is largely translated text (translationese), so the information conveyed across languages may not be exactly the same, and the authors have no way to measure these differences.
OpenAI has not released details of ChatGPT's training data, so the authors cannot ascertain the actual language statistics and must estimate them with CC100.
